rewrites.summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these countries."

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented rather than hypothetical: in September 2018 a Salalah court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and publishing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video — the judicial outcome of the January 2018 police arrests under the Penal Code's Article 22, which penalises appearing in female clothing or demeanour. A gender-nonconforming visitor detected on arrival can therefore be jailed, and nothing in the sources records where inside the prison system such prisoners are held.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Comparisons with neighbours: sources note the explicit anti-trans statute is unusual in its region, and the traveller's public warning told others "do not go to these countries." The national enforcement pattern is active — the 2018 arrests were publicly announced after private-party photos circulated on social media, showing active monitoring of gender non-conformity.

The September 2018 sentences completed the documented enforcement loop: eight months after the January 2018 police arrests, the Salalah preliminary court convicted the four men under Article 22 of the July 2018 Penal Code — which allows up to one year's imprisonment and an OMR 3,000 fine for "any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor" — with the stiffer three- and four-year sentences carrying additional charges for publishing immoral acts on social media. Court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people is the recorded pattern, not an isolated event.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The current sources record no resident-specific facts beyond the enforcement pattern already described in the summary — the 2018 arrests and the anti-trans statute apply to residents and visitors alike; no local cultural or resident-life facts are documented.

The four men sentenced in September 2018 were residents, and their convictions document how the state treats gender-nonconforming people inside its criminal system and what its courts order by way of imprisonment and fines — a pattern a detained visitor would meet from the inside.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: the airport account rests on a single traveller's first-hand account and could not be independently verified from the current sources, and whether the anti-trans statute has been applied at border entry for other travellers is not documented beyond that reported incident.

Prison axis: no Omani rule, practice or case is documented on where trans or gender-nonconforming prisoners are housed — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary or segregation practice. That absence cannot be read as a protected standard in a state that criminalises cross-dressing and has jailed people for it.
rewrites.notes: rt003 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (Roya News 2018-09-19 — Article 22 convictions of four men, three- and four-year sentences with OMR 3,000 fines; no housing-placement information) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming. Even the custody consequence axis is comparatively benign: at a 2023 parliamentary hearing the National Rehabilitation Institute's director stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to go to a men's or women's prison, trans women are currently placed in women's prisons, and a dedicated trans sector was planned for a new Montevideo prison — though he conceded the gap: "the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line."
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2013 (Latin America's first) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Prison-policy signals: the commitment to a dedicated trans sector in the planned Montevideo prison came with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system calling it "good news for a very vulnerable population" and estimating it would be ready in less than two years, and the rehabilitation institute told parliament that the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population — announced infrastructure, not yet delivered.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-declaration LGR, reparation pension, and state employment quota under Law 19,684 are resident-facing; the Joana killing and the hospital/bank discrimination incidents concerned residents.

Custody practice is resident-facing: official figures from the Parliamentary Commissioner's office count 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty; trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation is described as entailing "a whole process" of adaptation, and the planned trans sector of the new Montevideo prison would serve people already inside the system — a visitor meets all of this only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory.
Prison axis: the dedicated trans sector and Punta de Rieles accommodation were commitments announced in July 2023 (commissioner's estimate: ready within two years); nothing in the current sources documents whether delivery has occurred, and no source records special-unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners beyond the planned sector.
rewrites.notes: rt003 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (MercoPress 2023-07-29 — trans inmates choose men's or women's prison, trans women held in female prisons, dedicated trans sector planned, 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 deprived of liberty) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies. If a visitor is detained, the documented custody picture is structural and thin: as of a January 2015 reform proposal — never enacted — the prison system had no housing wing matched to gender identity, so transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, and no enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in two search rounds.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
No trans-specific killing has been documented here, in contrast to several neighbouring countries. The September 2025 cancellations of the flagship Pride march and other LGBTQ events in the largest city — a national-level policy signal that may colour a visit — are adjacent climate rather than a direct travel restriction.

The January 2015 separate-jails proposal is the only prison-axis document in the sources: the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute asked the Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners apart from the general population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing US state data that 67% of such prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey in which most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails — a reform bid with no enacted outcome recorded.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The stalled Gender Affirmation Law, the documented conversion efforts, and the healthcare discrimination barriers are resident-facing — these govern residents' access to recognition, safety, and care rather than a visitor's experience.

The placement finding concerns resident prisoners: in 2015 the only housing options documented for transgender prisoners were solitary confinement or the general population, because no wing matched their gender identity, and a 2014 survey found most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails — resident-facing conditions a visitor meets only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Political controls of one ruling party, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon or monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical effect of the stalled recognition law on border document checks is not documented in the sources.

Prison axis: the placement finding (solitary confinement or general population only, no identity-matched wing) dates from January 2015 and comes from a never-enacted reform proposal; two search rounds found no enacted outcome and no newer documented placement practice, so today's practice is unknown — and that unknown cannot be read as a protected standard in a state with no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.
rewrites.notes: rt003 VIS: folded verified prison-axis source (VietnamNet 2015-01-16 — solitary-or-general-population placement finding, unenacted separate-jails proposal, no newer practice documented) into visible fields as thin-data consequence evidence per LANE_SPECS rule 8b; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law. The lag is documented, with an improving record: in May 2018 the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each after finding the authorities had "knowingly and repeatedly" held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers and suffered insults and "continuous sexual abuse and violence"; since the 2013 gender-law reform, trans and gender-diverse inmates transfer to the female section and now receive individual cells there, though a 2024 University of Malta study still records misgendering by officers and clothing and healthcare gaps.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Litigation flux at the border: in July 2025 an international-court intervention was filed concerning an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in 2023 and facing a removal order — direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at the borders of the nation, though an asylum context rather than the ordinary visitor pass-through, and its outcome is pending.

The 2018 damages ruling is the prison-axis legal record: the civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded each of the seven women €4,000 for breach of rights and €1,000 for damage to personal dignity, ordered the director of prisons to pay, and the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the claimants — a binding judicial finding that prison authorities knowingly and repeatedly placed the inmates at high risk of sexual and psychological violence, with transfer to the female section refused in practice because it would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-determination legal gender recognition regime and passport 'X' markers are resident-facing administrative law; the prison healthcare and placement gaps concern resident inmates, with institutional practice found out of sync with national gender-identity law. A regional residents' survey ranks workers here top for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

The custody record concerns residents: the seven 2018 claimants stayed in the male section because transfer to the female section would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, while female inmates and warders were said to be hostile; current practice — transfer to the female section with individual cells, following earlier segregation in a separate dormitory (staff rationale: "the risks of pregnancies") — governs resident inmates, not visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general regional terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

Routine border handling of trans visitors is not documented beyond the asylum-seeker case, and no source describes visa or document scrutiny for trans visitors specifically.

Prison axis: the 2024 study rests on four interviews spanning 25 years; the earlier separate-dormitory segregation is documented from that study alone; no source in this record documents current solitary or special-unit practice for trans prisoners beyond what the study describes, and the abuse documented in the 2018 ruling predates the post-2013 reform practice.
rewrites.notes: rt003 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (Malta Today 2018-05-29 ruling — €5,000 each to seven inmates after "knowingly and repeatedly" high-risk male-section placement; University of Malta 2024 study — post-2013 female-section transfer, individual cells, residual misgendering and clothing/healthcare gaps) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.

rewrites.summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors: official WorldPride 2026 guidance confirms visas and entry depend only on nationality, not gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed at the border. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and since July 2025 a discriminatory motive is a statutory aggravating factor that can increase penalties by up to a third.

Practical safety supports are strong: Amsterdam operates dedicated reporting networks for LGBTQIA+ incidents, the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents for 2026, and the capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime. Same-sex marriage is legal and non-binary people are recognised, so a trans traveller's partner status raises no border or legal problems.

The genuine caution is rising reported hostility: discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people reached 4,800 last year, up 51% in a year for transgender-specific reports and 81% since 2022, and many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this chiefly means a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger. If a visitor is nonetheless detained, the custody consequence axis is a documented legal gap: no statute or regulation governs where transgender detainees are held — the Penitentiary Principles Act separates only male and female detainees — and the prison service places detainees by the gender designation in municipal records plus case-by-case factors (including the detainee's own preference), with transgender detainees frequently held on an "Extra Care Facility" wing alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders; courts have treated a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier, and a February 2024 human-rights lawyers' advisory called the unregulated placement "worrying and undesirable".
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
National policy turbulence is pending rather than in force: a self-identification gender-recognition bill was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; neither currently changes the border or discrimination rules a visitor faces.

Comparative context: the nation ranks #13 on a comparative rights map and #2 of 121 regions as a "good place", with public support at 52%; at the same time there is no statutory definition of "hate crime" at national level, the police recording hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a dedicated expertise centre.

Custody-policy flux: the national human-rights lawyers' committee (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection in February 2024 that no law, regulation or official policy governs transgender detainees' placement; the prison service confirmed placement by municipal-record gender plus case-by-case factors, the custodial-institutions agency said it was drafting guidelines that remained unpublished as of the sources, and the advisory urged rules aligned with Council of Europe CPT standards — policy in motion rather than in force.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The legal gender-recognition (LGR) process still requires an expert letter, falling short of self-determination: the self-identification bill (Transgender Act) was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months — all resident-facing.

Resident-facing victimisation data: official figures record that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people report physical or sexual violence (17% of trans respondents, 22% of intersex people), a third of police discrimination reports in 2022 concerned sexual orientation, only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were recorded last year, and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection.

The placement practice governs detained residents: the documented cases include a trans woman first held on a regular male wing at arrival, then moved to an Extra Care Facility wing; a 2016 parole-board appeals ruling on a trans woman placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation while there; and 2017 and 2020 sentencing rulings (Limburg district court; The Hague appeals court) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier — a visitor meets this only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Pickpocketing, bike theft and taxi scams are general tourist risks affecting everyone, including in the capital, Amsterdam.

Unresolved: the reporting platform describes its Pride-period figure (70+ reports) as "only a fraction of the total", so true incident volume is unverified; the documented enforcement gap (six convictions against 4,800 reports) is real but its practical effect on visitors is unquantified.

Prison axis: there are no official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, the frequency of Extra Care Facility placement is unquantified, and the guidelines the custodial-institutions agency was drafting as of February 2024 remain unpublished in the sources — current placement decisions rest on the documented case-by-case practice, not on a published standard.
rewrites.notes: rt003 VIS: folded 2 verified prison-axis sources (NJCM advisory 2024-02-22 and letter 2024-02-21 — no statutory placement rule, municipal-record plus case-by-case placement, Extra Care Facility wing practice, 2016-2020 rulings) into visible fields as consequence-axis evidence; existing claims preserved; no external research.
